## Intuition

The **change-of-variables** (or **transformation**) formula is a central tool
in multivariate calculus and probability. It states how integrals - and in
particular probability densities - transform under smooth, invertible maps.

It is the multivariate analogue of the one-dimensional substitution rule
$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_{\phi(a)}^{\phi(b)} f(\phi^{-1}(y))\,
\bigl|(\phi^{-1})'(y)\bigr|\,dy.
$$
In higher dimensions the derivative is replaced by the determinant of the
[[jacobian-and-hessian|Jacobian matrix]], which encodes how volume is
distorted.

Locally, a smooth map $T$ behaves like a **linear transformation**,
$$
T(x + h) \approx T(x) + J_{T}(x)h.
$$
A small volume element $dx$ near $x$ is sent to a distorted parallelepiped near
$T(x)$ of volume $|\det J_{T}(x)|\,dx$. The Jacobian determinant is the *local
volume-scaling factor*.

## Statement

:::{.theorem data-title="Change of Variables (Deterministic Form)"}

Let $U, V \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a $C^1$
bijection with $C^1$ inverse, $y = T(x)$. Then for any integrable
$f : V \to \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\int_V f(y)\,dy = \int_U f(T(x))\,\bigl|\det J_{T}(x)\bigr|\,dx,
$$
where $J_{T}(x)$ is the Jacobian matrix of $T$ at $x$. Equivalently, for
integrable $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\int_U g(x)\,dx = \int_V g(T^{-1}(y))\,\bigl|\det J_{T^{-1}}(y)\bigr|\,dy.
$$

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Change of Variables (Probabilistic Form)"}

Let $X$ be a random vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with density $f_X$ and let
$Y = T(X)$, where $T$ satisfies the assumptions above. Then $Y$ has density
$$
f_Y(y) = f_X(T^{-1}(y))\,\bigl|\det J_{T^{-1}}(y)\bigr|.
$$

:::

This preserves probabilities: $\mathbb{P}(Y \in A) = \mathbb{P}(X \in
T^{-1}(A))$. See also [[random-variable-transformations]].

## Proof (Sketch)

We prove the deterministic version.

1. **Linear case.** If $T(x) = Ax$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$
   invertible, then for any measurable $E$,
   $\mathrm{Vol}(A E) = |\det A|\,\mathrm{Vol}(E)$. Hence
   $$
   \int_{A U} f(y)\,dy=\int_U f(Ax)\,|\det A|\,dx.
   $$

2. **Local linearisation.** For general $C^1$ maps, near each $x$,
   $T(x+h) = T(x) + J_{T}(x)h + o(\lVert h\rVert)$. On a fine partition of $U$
   into small cells $C_k$, $T$ is well approximated on each $C_k$ by its
   linearisation at some point $x_k \in C_k$.

3. **Riemann sums.** Writing the integral as a limit of Riemann sums,
   $$
   \int_V f(y)\,dy \approx \sum_k f(T(x_k))\,\mathrm{Vol}(T(C_k))
   \approx \sum_k f(T(x_k))\,|\det J_{T}(x_k)|\,\mathrm{Vol}(C_k).
   $$
   Letting the mesh go to zero gives the formula.

A fully rigorous proof uses measure-theoretic arguments and the inverse
function theorem.

## Examples

:::{.example data-title="Polar Coordinates"}

Let $T(r,\theta) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$. Then
$$
J_{T}(r,\theta) = \begin{pmatrix}
\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \\
\sin\theta & r\cos\theta
\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det J_{T}(r,\theta) = r,
$$
so
$$
\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x,y)\,dx\,dy = \int_0^\infty \int_0^{2\pi}
f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\, r\, d\theta\, dr.
$$
In probability, if $(R,\Theta)$ has joint density $g(r,\theta)$, then
$f_{X,Y}(x,y) = g(r,\theta)/r$ at $(x,y) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Linear Transformation of a Gaussian"}

Let $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ and $Y = AX$ with $A$ invertible. Then
$T^{-1}(y)=A^{-1}y$ and $|\det J_{T^{-1}}(y)| = 1/|\det A|$, so
$$
f_Y(y) = (2\pi)^{-d/2}
\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 \lVert A^{-1}y\rVert^2\right)\frac{1}{|\det A|},
$$
which is exactly the density of $\mathcal{N}(0, AA^\top)$.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Ratio of Two Independent Variables"}

Let $X,Y$ be independent with joint density $f_{X,Y}$, and define
$U = X/Y$, $V = Y$. Then $T(x,y) = (x/y, y)$ and $T^{-1}(u,v) = (uv, v)$ with
$$
J_{T^{-1}}(u,v) = \begin{pmatrix}
v & u \\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det J_{T^{-1}} = v.
$$
Hence $f_{U,V}(u,v) = f_{X,Y}(uv, v)\,|v|$, and marginalising over $v$ gives
the density of $U = X/Y$.

:::
